questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a dramaturg does
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a dramaturg's role consists of
questions.stem: At the study group's revision session, Priya claims that the dramaturg's job is to make the production's thinking legible. Which claim best captures that role?

options.text: It is to write the programme note, since audiences need the production explained to them
options.misconception: reduces the role to publicity writing

options.text: It is to choose the designer, since the concept must be carried by someone visible
options.misconception: treats the role as casting a designer

options.text: It is to test the production's thinking against the text and keep the whole visible to the team
It is to manage the rehearsal schedule, since ideas need deadlines to survive
options.misconception: makes the role administrative

questions.explanation: The dramaturg works between text and production, testing what the staging is doing against what the text does. Keeping the production's ideas visible to the whole team is the substance of the job, not writing notes or scheduling.
questions.hint: Ask what the role holds in view.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A concept statement and what it commits to
questions.learningObjective: Infer what a concept statement commits a production to

stimulus.body: The group's concept note for their production of a late Victorian murder mystery states that the household is a machine for producing guilt, and that every scene should be staged so that the machinery is visible. The note asks for a drawing-room set with the pipes of the heating system left exposed.

questions.stem: In the study note about the household as machinery, the request for exposed heating pipes commits the production to what?

options.text: Realism, since exposing the pipes makes the set more accurate than a concealed one
options.misconception: reads the choice as a demand for realism

options.text: Naturalism, since Victorian heating cannot be hidden in any accurate setting
options.misconception: reduces the commitment to period accuracy

options.text: Modernity, since exposed services are a contemporary taste
options.misconception: reads the choice as a modern fashion

options.text: The idea that the house works mechanically to produce guilt, made visible in the set itself

questions.explanation: The concept treats the house as a machine for producing guilt, so exposing the pipes makes the idea visible rather than decorative. The choice commits the production to showing its argument, not to accuracy for its own sake.
questions.hint: Ask what the note is trying to show.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A design element and the meaning it carries
questions.learningObjective: Identify a design element that carries meaning
questions.stem: During the revision session, Tomo argues that a design element carries meaning into the production. Which example best illustrates that claim?

options.text: A cracked mirror in the dressing room, made visible so the house's divided loyalties have a shape
A cracked mirror, chosen because real mirrors in that period were often cracked
options.misconception: treats the choice as period accuracy alone

options.text: A cracked mirror, ordered last because the director wanted the image discovered by chance
options.misconception: credits the choice to accident

options.text: A cracked mirror, added because the set designer had one left over from another show
options.misconception: grounds the choice in leftover stock

questions.explanation: A design element carries meaning when the choice refers to the production's argument rather than to accuracy, convenience or accident. The cracked mirror works here because it gives a visible form to the play's theme of divided loyalty.
questions.hint: Ask what the element refers to.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A concept statement and what it commits to
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a concept statement commits a production to
questions.stem: In the study group's revision, Sam is asked to explain what a concept statement commits a production to. Write the answer she needs.

answer.exemplar: A concept statement commits the production to a single organising idea that the staging must express rather than merely accompany. It settles what the play is being made to say, and every element afterwards is judged by whether it serves that idea. The commitment is real but not absolute: a statement guides choices and can be revised when the work proves better than the plan.

questions.explanation: The answer must define the concept as an organising idea that elements must serve, and note that it guides rather than fixes. The exemplar does both.
questions.hint: Say what every element must serve.

questions.topic: A concept statement and what it commits to
questions.learningObjective: Defend a concept statement over a collection of impressions
questions.stem: At the revision meeting, Lena argues that a concept statement is more useful than a mood board. Which argument supports her?

options.text: Because a mood board is cheaper to make, so the committee should spend its budget on rehearsal time
options.misconception: grounds the argument in budgeting

options.text: Because a concept commits the team to something arguable, while a mood board only records impressions
Because directors prefer concepts, since the form flatters their authority in the room
options.misconception: attacks the form by suggesting vanity

options.text: Because mood boards are used by designers, and designers should not shape a production's thinking
options.misconception: sets designers against the production's thinking

questions.explanation: The argument rests on what the two documents can be used for. A concept gives the team something to disagree with and to test, while a board of impressions records taste without committing anyone to a claim.
questions.hint: Ask which document can be argued with.

questions.topic: A lighting cue and what it withholds
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise what a lighting cue can withhold
questions.stem: In the group's revision, Kai argues that a lighting cue can withhold as well as reveal. Which set of claims follows?

options.text: A cue can hide a face, hide a letter and hide a figure standing in the wings
options.misconception: reduces the cue's work to hiding things

options.text: A cue can show a face, show a letter and show a figure waiting offstage
options.misconception: limits the cue to revelation

options.text: A cue can fix a mood, fix a colour and fix the temperature of the whole production
options.misconception: makes the cue purely atmospheric

options.text: A cue can isolate a face, keep a letter unread and leave an audience uncertain about what it saw

questions.explanation: Withholding is part of a lighting cue's work, since it selects what the audience is given and holds back what it is not. The claims that follow treat the cue as managing the audience's knowledge rather than their mood.

questions.learningObjective: Describe what a sound cue does at a transition
questions.stem: Regarding transitions, Ravi asks what a sound cue does at a transition. Which account is most accurate?

options.text: It fills the silence between scenes, since a pause always needs covering
options.misconception: treats the cue as a filler for silence

options.text: It announces the next scene, since audiences need warning of what follows
options.misconception: makes the cue a signpost

options.text: It marks the change of time or place, so the audience accepts a new situation
It signals to the crew that a changeover is beginning, since sound leads the action
options.misconception: makes the cue a technical signal

questions.explanation: A sound cue at a transition occupies the boundary between two situations, so the audience accepts the shift without being told. It marks the change rather than filling a gap, and it acts on where the audience believes it is.

options.text: Improving the text, since good dialogue matters more than anything a designer does

options.text: Testing coherence, since the whole staging must express one idea rather than several
Protecting the designer, since the concept belongs to the person who supplied it

Because an arguable concept allows the director to change the production's mind easily

options.misconception: grounds the claim in scheduling

answer.exemplar: A design element carries meaning when it belongs to the production's argument rather than to the era or to convenience. options.misconception: relies on audience recognition alone

questions.explanation: Costume signals social position, wealth, occupation and period at a glance, and it does so before a character speaks. That makes it a form of information the production can use, not decoration applied to a finished design.

questions.stem: In the revision meeting, Ollie asks whether a stage property must be realistic to be useful. Which answer is best?

options.text: It must be realistic, since an audience reads a false object as a mistake
options.misconception: makes realism a condition of usefulness

options.text: It must be minimal, since audiences notice props more than they notice actors
options.misconception: claims props overshadow the actors

options.text: It need only be legible and chosen deliberately, since its detail is read as meaning
It should be invisible, since a well-used prop is one the audience never sees
options.misconception: values invisibility over meaning

questions.explanation: A property earns its place when the audience can read it and when its choice has been thought about, not because every detail is exact. Deliberateness in what is shown can carry more meaning than accuracy.

questions.topic: A lighting cue and what it withholds
questions.learningObjective: Identify an example of a lighting cue withholding
questions.stem: While revising the lighting plan, Hana asks what a lighting cue can withhold. Which example best shows it?

options.text: A single lamp left on a figure's face while the room darkens, keeping one expression readable
A blackout at the end of the scene, hiding the set from view for the interval
options.misconception: claims the blackout is withholding information

options.text: A flood of white light on the stage, obscuring the scene's dimmest details
options.misconception: treats brightness as withholding

options.text: A colour change from warm to cold, hiding the fact that the time of day has shifted
options.misconception: calls a colour change concealment

questions.explanation: Withholding means deciding what the audience is not given to see, and the single lamp does that by keeping one face lit while the rest goes dark. A blackout ends the scene; a colour change signals time.
questions.hint: Ask what stays hidden in the dark.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A sound cue and the transition it marks
questions.learningObjective: Infer what a continuous sound accomplishes across a scene change

stimulus.body: The group's notes describe a sound cue: a train that runs under the scene in the middle of a domestic argument and continues for the whole of the next scene. The note records that the actors found they could no longer tell where the first scene ended and the second began.

questions.stem: The running-train note in the group's papers records that the actors could no longer tell where one scene ended and the next began. What has the sound cue accomplished?

options.text: It blurred the boundary, so the change of scene was accepted without a break being felt
It confused the actors, which shows the cue needed to be shortened before the next show
options.misconception: reads the effect as a rehearsal problem

options.text: It marked the change of location, since a train can only exist near a railway
options.misconception: limits the cue to a literal location signal

options.text: It drowned out the dialogue, so the second scene's argument was never heard
options.misconception: claims the cue suppressed the dialogue

questions.explanation: The train runs through the boundary, so the audience never registers the seam between the scenes. The cue makes the transition acceptable rather than marking it, and the actors' uncertainty shows the effect.
questions.hint: Ask where the seam disappeared.

questions.stem: When the group revises the set, Jonah asks what makes a stage property realistic. Which answer is sound?

options.text: It is realistic when it looks exactly like the object in the period, down to its wear
options.misconception: defines realism as visual accuracy alone

options.text: It is realistic when the audience believes it could be used, since belief is the test
options.misconception: reduces realism to audience belief

It is realistic when it was made by a real craftsman, since workmanship cannot be faked
options.misconception: grounds realism in manufacture

questions.explanation: Realism in a property is judged by whether it works under the conditions the scene imposes: it must bear weight, make sound and hold a shape as the play uses it. Visual accuracy alone does not make a prop usable or convincing.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a slow fade is made to communicate

stimulus.body: The group's lighting plan for the final scene specifies a slow fade from full daylight to the colour of a single gas lamp over ninety seconds, with no other change to the room. The note says the audience should feel the house itself grow older.

options.text: To show the passage of hours, since a fade always measures elapsed time
options.misconception: treats the fade as a clock

options.text: To hide the scene change, since the audience cannot see a change in a fade

questions.topic: A lighting cue and what it withholds
questions.learningObjective: Identify a further thing a lighting cue can withhold
questions.stem: On what lighting can keep back, Marta asks what a lighting cue can withhold beyond a face. Which is the best example?

options.misconception: treats the cue as hiding a shape alone

options.text: A bright beam that shows the whole set, leaving the audience nothing to imagine
options.misconception: claims brightness withholds imagination

answer.exemplar: A property is realistic when it holds up under the conditions the scene imposes. questions.topic: A lighting cue and what it withholds
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a lighting cue can withhold about expectation
questions.stem: On the question of expectation, Tobi asks what a lighting cue can withhold from the audience. Which answer is most accurate?

options.text: It can withhold the actor's face, since a face is the only thing audiences seek
options.misconception: claims faces are the only object of attention

options.text: It can withhold the sound of the scene, since lighting and sound are one system
options.misconception: mixes lighting with sound

options.text: It can withhold what the audience expects next, since what is lit sets what they anticipate
It can withhold the length of the performance, since the count of cues fixes the running time
options.misconception: claims cue count fixes running time

questions.explanation: Light shapes expectation, because what is lit reads as what is about to matter. By controlling that, a cue can hold back the direction of the audience's attention, keeping the scene's expectation unsettled.
questions.hint: Ask what the lit area promises.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A sound cue and the transition it marks
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a sound spanning two scenes achieves

stimulus.body: The group's notes on the final transition record that the sound of a key in a lock begins in the previous scene and finishes in the next one, where it is a different door in a different street. The note says the audience should not be troubled by the move.

questions.stem: The key-and-door note records a sound that begins in one scene and finishes in another. What is the transition cue doing?

options.text: Bridging the seam, so the sound carries the audience across the change without a jolt
Announcing the new location, since a key sound always tells the audience where they are
options.misconception: makes the cue a location marker

options.text: Confirming the passage of time, since a key turning always takes a measurable moment
options.misconception: makes the cue a time marker

options.text: Covering the changeover, since the set change cannot be heard over the sound
options.misconception: treats the cue as covering noise

questions.explanation: A sound that begins in one scene and finishes in another occupies both sides of the seam, so the audience crosses the boundary rather than stopping at it. The transition is continuous rather than jarring.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the seam it occupies.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a dramaturg does
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a dramaturg reads the text more than once
questions.stem: On the question of reading, Priya asks why the dramaturg reads the text more than once. Which answer is best?

options.text: Because the second reading reveals what the first reading took for granted
Because the script may be revised, so the text must be rechecked before each run
options.misconception: grounds the re-reading in revision policy

options.text: Because the actors need help with their parts, so somebody must check the lines
options.misconception: makes the role an acting coach

options.text: Because the licence requires the text to be read twice before it is approved
options.misconception: invents a licensing requirement

questions.explanation: A first reading follows the story, while a second can notice what the story assumed. That difference is what a dramaturg needs, since the work is to see the habits a production has picked up from the text.
questions.hint: Ask what the second reading catches.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A concept statement and what it commits to
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a concept statement commits a production to
questions.stem: Writing his answer, Femi is asked what a concept statement commits a production to. Write it out.

answer.exemplar: A concept statement commits the production to one organising idea that the staging must express rather than decorate. It tells the team what the play is being made to say, and it gives them a standard by which to judge each choice that follows. Because it is written to be argued with, the statement stays open to revision, but no element may quietly set itself against it.

questions.explanation: The answer must define the concept as an organising idea and a standard for judging choices, and note that it can be revised. The exemplar covers both.
questions.hint: Say what it judges the choices by.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A design element and the meaning it carries
questions.learningObjective: Defend the claim that a production should hold one design idea
questions.stem: On the question of design unity, Solomon argues that a production should have one design idea, not several. Which argument is best?

options.text: Because several ideas pull the audience's attention apart, and a production's force depends on holding one
Because designers charge less when they are given a single instruction
options.misconception: grounds the claim in design fees

options.text: Because one idea is easier to put in the programme note and advertise
options.misconception: grounds the claim in publicity

options.text: Because several ideas always mean the production is confused about its own text
options.misconception: confuses plurality with confusion

questions.explanation: The argument puts the value of one idea in the audience's attention, which must be gathered somewhere. Competing designs spend it on their differences, so the production loses the force of insistence.
questions.hint: Ask where the attention goes.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Costume as a period signal
questions.learningObjective: Identify what costume can say that dialogue cannot
questions.stem: In the group's final revision, Nadia asks what costume can say that the dialogue cannot. Which claim is best?

options.text: It can say what a character intends, since costume shows the plan behind the words
options.misconception: claims costume reveals intention

options.text: It can say what the audience should feel, since colour decides the emotional response
options.misconception: makes costume a mood control

options.text: It can say what a character's position is, since cut and fabric mark it before speech
It can say what will happen later, since costume often foreshadows coming events
options.misconception: treats costume as foreshadowing

questions.explanation: Costume states a character's place in the world through cut, fabric and colour, before the character has said anything. Dialogue can qualify that position later, but it cannot come first in the same way.
questions.hint: Ask what costume states before speech.
